seo_title: What Insurance Policies Include an Appraisal Clause?
meta_description: Which insurance policies include an appraisal clause? Homeowners, commercial, auto and flood policies, and how to find yours.
h1: What Insurance Policies Include an Appraisal Clause?
secondary_keywords: does my policy have an appraisal clause
excerpt: Most homeowners, condo, renters, dwelling, and commercial property policies include an appraisal clause. Learn which policies do, which don't, and how to find yours.
key_takeaways: Most first-party property policies, including homeowners and commercial, include appraisal.
Many auto and flood policies include appraisal provisions with their own rules.
Liability, health, and life policies generally do not include appraisal.
Find the clause in your policy's conditions section and check every endorsement.
body_html:
Most first-party property policies include an appraisal clause, including homeowners, condo, renters, dwelling, and commercial property policies, and many auto policies include one for physical damage. Liability, health, and life insurance policies generally do not. The clause lets either side resolve disputes over the amount of a covered loss through appraisers and an umpire.

If you are fighting over a claim payment, one of the first questions to answer is whether your policy gives you the right to appraisal. In Texas, the answer for most property owners is yes. But the wording, the triggers, and the limits differ from policy to policy, and a few policy types follow their own procedures.

This guide covers which insurance policies typically include an appraisal clause, which usually do not, how to find the clause in your policy, and when invoking it makes sense.

What Is an Appraisal Clause in an Insurance Policy?

An appraisal clause is a policy condition that provides a method for resolving disagreements about the amount of loss without going to court. Typical language says that if you and the insurer fail to agree on the amount of loss, either party may demand appraisal in writing. Each side then selects a competent and independent (or disinterested) appraiser, the appraisers select an umpire, and an agreement by any two of the three sets the amount of loss.

Appraisal usually decides: repair and replacement costs, scope of damage, quantities, pricing, and the extent of damage caused by a covered event.

Appraisal usually does not decide: whether the policy covers the loss, whether exclusions apply, or whether the insurer acted in bad faith. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), those coverage and liability questions remain for the insurer and the courts. Learn the basics in what is an insurance appraisal.

Which Insurance Policies Include an Appraisal Clause?

The table below summarizes common policy types. Always confirm with your actual policy, because forms and endorsements vary.

Policy typeAppraisal clause?Typical disputes
Homeowners (HO-3, Texas HO-B and similar forms)Usually yesRoof, hail, wind, water, fire, matching
Condo (HO-6) and renters (HO-4)Usually yesInterior finishes, personal property values
Dwelling / landlord policiesUsually yesRental property damage
Commercial propertyUsually yesRoofs, building damage, business personal property
Business income (when part of a commercial property form)Often yesLost income calculations
Personal auto (physical damage)Often yesVehicle value, repair cost
Flood (NFIP and private)Often yes, with its own rulesAmount of flood loss
Liability, health, and lifeGenerally noHandled through other dispute processes

Homeowners Insurance Policies and Appraisal

Nearly all standard homeowners policies sold in Texas include an appraisal condition. It applies to the dwelling, other structures, and personal property coverages. For Texas homeowners, the most common appraisal disputes involve:

  • Hail and wind damage to roofs, siding, and windows
  • Repair versus full roof replacement
  • Water damage scope, including drying, drywall, flooring, and cabinets
  • Fire and smoke damage cleaning versus replacement
  • Matching of siding, flooring, or shingles
  • Pricing and missing line items in the carrier's estimate

If your roof claim is the issue, see can appraisal be used for roof claims.

Commercial Property Insurance Policies and Appraisal

Standard commercial property forms also include an appraisal condition. Commercial disputes tend to be larger and more complex, covering multiple buildings, specialized roofing systems, tenant improvements, equipment, and inventory. Apartment complexes, HOAs, churches, retail centers, and industrial facilities all regularly use appraisal. For community associations, see our guide to the HOA insurance appraisal process.

When business income coverage is written as part of the commercial property policy, the appraisal clause may reach disputes about lost income, though the calculations require accounting expertise in addition to construction estimating. Read more in commercial property insurance appraisal in Texas.

Auto and Flood Policies With Appraisal Provisions

Auto insurance

Many personal auto policies include an appraisal provision for physical damage claims, typically disputes over a vehicle's actual cash value after a total loss or the cost of repairs. Auto appraisal follows a similar two-appraisers-and-umpire structure.

Flood insurance

Flood policies, including those issued through the National Flood Insurance Program, generally include an appraisal provision for disagreements over the amount of a covered flood loss. NFIP claims also follow federal rules and deadlines, so review your policy and FEMA's flood insurance guidance carefully.

Texas windstorm (TWIA) policies

Texas Windstorm Insurance Association policies on the coast follow a separate statutory claims process with its own dispute resolution procedures and deadlines. If you have a TWIA policy, read its claim provisions closely rather than assuming a standard appraisal clause applies.

Which Insurance Policies Usually Do Not Include Appraisal?

  • Liability policies. Disputes involve third-party claims and the duty to defend, not a property valuation.
  • Health insurance. Disputes use internal appeals and external review processes.
  • Life insurance. Benefits are set amounts, so there is no "amount of loss" to appraise.
  • Some specialty or surplus lines policies, which may replace appraisal with arbitration or omit it entirely.

If your policy lacks an appraisal clause, you still have options: negotiating with documentation, requesting a reinspection, filing a complaint with the Texas Department of Insurance, mediation, or legal action. Those paths are usually slower than appraisal, which is one reason the clause is so valuable when it exists.

Appraisal is also different from arbitration. An arbitration clause may give an arbitrator authority over broader issues, including coverage. Appraisal is limited to the amount of loss.

How to Find the Appraisal Clause in Your Policy

  1. Get your complete policy, including the declarations page, the policy form, and all endorsements. Your agent or insurer must provide it on request.
  2. Look in the conditions section. In homeowners forms, appraisal usually appears under "Section I Conditions." In commercial forms, it is typically under "Loss Conditions."
  3. Search for the word "appraisal." In a PDF, a quick search finds it in seconds.
  4. Check endorsements. Some endorsements modify or replace the standard appraisal language, including how appraisers and umpires are chosen.
  5. Note the details: how to demand appraisal, deadlines to name appraisers, how the umpire is selected, and how costs are split.
Tip: Texas policies sometimes use specific phrases such as "competent and disinterested" or "independent" to describe appraisers. That language affects who can serve as your appraiser, so read it before you choose one.

When Should You Invoke the Appraisal Clause?

Appraisal is usually worth considering when:

  • The insurer accepts the loss is covered but pays far less than repairs will cost
  • Negotiations, supplements, and reinspections have stalled
  • The dispute is about scope, quantities, pricing, or repair versus replacement
  • The potential recovery justifies the cost of an appraiser and a share of the umpire

Appraisal does not guarantee a higher payment. The award reflects the evidence, and in some cases it lands closer to the insurer's number. Run the math first with our appraisal cost calculator, and review whether insurance appraisal increases settlement amounts.

Advantages of appraisal

  • Faster than litigation. Many appraisals finish in weeks or months rather than years.
  • Lower cost. Each side pays its own appraiser and splits the umpire, which is usually far less than a lawsuit.
  • Expert decision-makers. Appraisers and umpires understand construction, estimating, and pricing.
  • Binding result. An award signed by two of the three generally settles the amount of loss.

Limitations to understand

  • Coverage disputes continue. The insurer may still contest whether some items are covered.
  • Costs add up on complex losses that need engineers or multiple inspections.
  • Appraiser quality matters. An inexperienced appraiser or poorly chosen umpire can hurt the outcome.
  • Limited appeal. Courts generally set aside awards only for problems such as fraud, mistake, or appraisers exceeding their authority.

Choosing the right appraiser

Look for an appraiser who inspects damage personally, writes detailed Xactimate or Symbility estimates, understands Texas appraisal practice, and has no financial interest in the repairs. Joseph Dittman of TX Insurance Appraiser is a Texas-licensed public adjuster who serves as the policyholder's appraiser (or as umpire) on appraisal assignments, bringing years of policyholder-side claim experience to residential and commercial disputes.

Appraisal Clauses in Texas Property Claims

Appraisal is used heavily in Texas because the state sees frequent hail, wind, and tropical storm losses. After a major storm in the DFW Metroplex, Central Texas, or along the Gulf Coast near Houston, insurers process huge claim volumes, and scope disagreements follow.

Texas law also shapes appraisal. Texas courts generally enforce appraisal clauses as written. Insurers must meet prompt payment deadlines under Insurance Code chapter 542, and in Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), the Texas Supreme Court held that paying an appraisal award does not automatically bar a prompt-payment claim. This is general information, not legal advice.

Next Steps: Confirm Your Clause and Get a Second Opinion

Pull your full policy, find the appraisal condition, and note its procedures. Then compare the carrier's estimate with an independent estimate to measure the real gap. If the difference is significant and coverage is not in dispute, appraisal may be the most efficient way to resolve it.

Before you demand appraisal, gather the documents an appraiser will need:

  • The full certified policy with all endorsements
  • The insurer's estimate, photos, and any engineer or inspection reports
  • Your own photos, videos, and storm or loss documentation
  • Itemized contractor estimates and invoices for any emergency repairs
  • All letters, emails, and notes from calls with the adjuster

Having these ready speeds up the process and lets your appraiser identify the strongest issues from day one.

faqs.q: Do all homeowners insurance policies have an appraisal clause?
faqs.a: Most standard homeowners policies sold in Texas include an appraisal condition, but not every policy is identical. Some surplus lines or specialty policies modify, replace, or omit it. Always review the full policy, including endorsements, to confirm whether appraisal is available and what procedures and deadlines apply before you send a demand.

faqs.q: Where is the appraisal clause in my insurance policy?
faqs.a: In homeowners policies, the appraisal clause is usually listed under Section I Conditions. In commercial property policies, it typically appears in the Loss Conditions section. Searching the policy PDF for the word appraisal is the fastest way to find it. Also check endorsements, which can change how appraisers and umpires are chosen.

faqs.q: Is appraisal the same as arbitration?
faqs.a: No. Appraisal is limited to the amount of loss, such as repair costs and scope, and does not decide coverage. Arbitration clauses can give an arbitrator authority over broader issues, including coverage and policy interpretation. Some specialty policies use arbitration instead of appraisal, so read your policy carefully to know which process applies.

faqs.q: Can my insurance company force me into appraisal?
faqs.a: If your policy includes an appraisal clause, either side can generally demand appraisal when there is a genuine disagreement over the amount of loss. That means the insurer can invoke it too. Texas courts generally enforce appraisal clauses as written, though a party may challenge a demand if it was waived or the dispute is really about coverage.

faqs.q: Does renters or condo insurance include appraisal?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Renters (HO-4) and condo (HO-6) policies are built on homeowners forms and commonly include the same appraisal condition. For renters, disputes often involve personal property values. For condo owners, they may involve interior finishes and improvements, while the building itself is usually covered under the association's master policy.
